opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is that a lot of real-world tasks just can't be solved in one shot. If you think about how a person actually does research or debugs something, you don't know upfront exactly what you need. You take an action, you look at what comes back, and that changes what you do next.

Take something like answering a hard research question. Your first search gives you partial information, maybe it surfaces a name or a paper you didn't know about, and only then can you formulate the next query. Or in coding, you run the tests, you see a failure, you inspect a file, you make an edit, you rerun. Each step depends on the observation from the previous one. A single tool call, or even a fixed batch of parallel calls, can't capture that dependency structure.

So multi-turn tool use is really about letting the model interleave reasoning with interaction with the environment. The model has to decide what to do given what it's learned so far, recover when a tool returns something unexpected or an error, and know when it has enough information to stop. That's a qualitatively different skill from just picking the right function and filling in arguments.

And that's also why it's interesting from a training perspective. If you only train on single-turn tool calls, the model never learns things like backtracking, verifying intermediate results, or planning over a longer horizon. You need multi-turn trajectories, ideally with some kind of outcome-based signal, often via reinforcement learning, so the model learns that the sequence of actions as a whole led to a good result. That's where a lot of the capability for genuinely agentic behavior comes from.

r001.rationale: It explains that an action’s result changes what the model does next, with research and coding examples where later tool calls depend on earlier observations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we think about what makes an agent an agent, as opposed to just a model answering a question, the key thing is that it has to interact with an environment. And most real environments don't give you everything you need in one shot. If you think about something like booking travel, or debugging a codebase, or even just answering a question that requires looking things up, the information you need to make the next decision often only becomes available after you've taken an action.

So a single tool call just isn't enough. You search for something, and the result tells you that you were asking the wrong question, or that there's a detail you didn't anticipate. Then you have to adjust and call another tool, maybe a different one, maybe the same one with different parameters. And this goes on for several steps. The model has to hold onto what it's learned so far, reason about what's still missing, and decide what to do next. That's fundamentally a multi-turn process.

The other thing I'd point out is that the hard part isn't really calling the tool. Most models can format a function call correctly at this point. The hard part is the planning and the recovery. When a tool returns an error, or returns something unexpected, does the model know how to recover? Does it know when it has enough information to stop? Does it avoid looping forever? Those behaviors only show up in multi-turn settings, and they're exactly the things that break in practice when you try to deploy these systems.

So from a research and training perspective, if you only evaluate or train on single-turn tool use, you're optimizing for a toy version of the problem. The real tasks that people actually want agents to do, the ones that have economic value, almost all require this kind of iterative, stateful interaction with tools. That's why we see it as necessary rather than nice-to-have.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a tool’s result can reveal what information is missing or change the question, requiring the agent to adjust and make another tool call.

astra-6.text:
Well, for many tasks, you don’t know all the steps upfront. You might need to call a tool, look at what comes back, and then decide what to do next. Maybe you’re searching for something, and the first result gives you a clue that lets you make a more specific query. Or you’re writing code, running it, seeing an error, and fixing it.

So it’s a feedback loop: take an action, observe the result, and adapt. A single round of tool calls works when the requests are independent and you already know what information you need. But when the next action depends on what you’ve just learned, you need multiple turns to actually complete the task.

r001.rationale: The response explains that an agent must inspect a tool’s result and adapt its next action, so the next tool-use turn depends on what the earlier call returned.

sol-6.1.text:
Some tasks require you to discover what to do as you go. You might call a tool, look at the result, and realize you need more information or need to take a different action. You can’t necessarily decide on all the tool calls up front, because the next step depends on what you learn from the previous one.

For example, if you’re investigating a problem, your first query might tell you where to look, but it won’t necessarily give you the answer. You need to follow up, test a hypothesis, and perhaps revise it. Multi-turn tool use gives an agent that feedback loop, so it can work through the task instead of being limited to a single attempt.

r001.rationale: It explains that an agent may need to inspect a tool result and choose a follow-up action based on what it learns, so the next tool call cannot always be decided in advance.
